title: Fabriq Developer vs Nango: What You Own and What You Call
summary: Free tiers, catalogue size, whose OAuth app you register, self-hosting, and who holds your user's token. First-party, checked 29 October 2026.
body_markdown:
TL;DR


**These two products answer different questions, and the free tiers give the difference away.** Nango's free plan is 10 connections, and its own FAQ defines a connection as one access token: "3 users connect their Gmail = 3 connections". Fabriq Developer's free plan is 20,000 calls a month with unlimited agents, priced on calls rather than on connected users — with one asterisk we got wrong the first time: on our free plan your users connect through an OAuth app *you* register, because Agentic Fabriq's shared provider apps are a paid-plan feature.


The second difference is what the word "open source" buys you. Nango's repository ships under the Elastic License 2.0, and the free self-hosted build covers auth and the proxy only. Syncs, tool calls and the MCP server require Nango Cloud or an enterprise self-host.


So the honest comparison isn't feature counts. It's whether you want to operate an integration platform or call one.


This is not an argument that Nango is the weaker product. If you want integration code you own and can read, if you need provider data replicated into your own database, or if your users have to see your company's name on the consent screen, Nango is the better buy today and we'll show you why below. An earlier version of this page implied Nango pushes you to register your own OAuth app before launch; its auth guide now says plainly that "Nango-managed OAuth apps can be used in production", and we have corrected that below.


Decide it on Friday with three questions: how many users will connect before you charge anyone, whether you need syncs, and whether you can afford to register OAuth apps with every provider before your first call.


**Published by Agentic Fabriq.** This is a first-party comparison: we make one of the two products on it, so read it as our argument rather than an independent test. We score neither product and we call nothing here independent. **Comparison checked: 29 October 2026.** Every Nango claim below links to Nango's own current pricing page, documentation or repository, with the date we read it; where a figure is not published on a primary source we say so instead of estimating, and where a figure or a recommendation has changed since our first reading we show both. Fabriq figures come from our own[pricing page](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/pricing) , the[Fabriq Developer page](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/developers) , the[Developer Quickstart](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/docs/dev-quickstart) , and the generated provider catalogue in our codebase.


## Overview


We've argued the governance side of this market twice, in[10 Best AI Agent Integration Platforms](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/best-ai-agent-integration-platforms) and[Composio alternatives](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/blog/composio-alternatives) . Both rank on agent identity, per-user authority and audit, because that's what a security review asks. This page doesn't. A two-person team at pre-seed has no security review. It has a Friday afternoon, a demo on Tuesday, and a worry about whether today's choice survives six months.


For that reader the decisive facts are narrow and boring. What the free tier actually covers. How many providers are reachable, and reachable *how* . How long until a tool call returns real data. Whether you have to register an OAuth app with Google before anything works. And who ends up holding your user's access token.


Nango and Agentic Fabriq both answer those questions, and they are not the same kind of product. Nango is an integration platform: unified auth, a proxy, functions you deploy, syncs that replicate provider data into a records cache, and webhooks. Its repository describes it as a way to "connect your agents & product to 1,000 APIs", and agent sessions expose your deployed functions to a model over MCP. Fabriq Developer is narrower. It's a hosted gateway that holds your users' credentials, attaches them server-side at call time, and serves tools to an agent over one MCP endpoint.


One of those you run. The other you call. That's the axis this page is about.


**The question underneath all of this:** are you buying infrastructure to operate, or a dependency to call? Nango will give you more control than Fabriq and ask you to do more work for it. Both answers are defensible. Picking the wrong one costs you a migration six months in.


## The Free Tiers Are Not Comparable


Start here. It's where the two diverge hardest and where most comparison pages wave a hand.


Nango's free plan is $0 a month with three limits: 10 connections, 10 hours of compute, 10GB of transfer. The first one decides everything, and Nango's pricing FAQ is direct about what it counts: "1 Connection = 1 API key or access token of the external API. For example: 3 users connect their Gmail = 3 connections." If your product asks for Gmail and Slack, every user costs two of your ten. Five users and you're done. Free-tier requests are also rate limited to 200 a minute, against 1,000 on the paid plan.


Past that, Pay-as-you-go is $50 a month base including $50 of monthly credits, then $0.29 per connection, $0.72 per hour of function compute and $0.50 per gigabyte of transfer, with connections prorated by how long they sit in your account. A thousand users with two tools each is 2,000 connections, or $580 a month before any compute.


Fabriq Developer's free plan is priced on a different unit. It's free forever with 20,000 API calls a month, unlimited agents, per-agent tool permissions, request logs, live sessions, and the Python SDK, the` afctl` CLI and the MCP endpoint. A call is any request your agent makes through Fabriq, which includes authenticating and retrieving credentials, not just the tool call itself. That unit is coarser than a tool call, and we'd rather say so than let you find out from an invoice. The paid steps are $50 a month for 200,000 calls and $300 a month for 2,000,000 ($2.50 and $1.50 per 10,000 included calls), with add-on calls at $2 per 10,000 on either paid plan.


The free plan's real limitation is not the call ceiling. It is that our shared provider apps sit behind a paid plan: on Free, your users authorize through an OAuth app you register, which is the same paperwork Nango's free plan asks of you if you choose your own app there.


The practical difference: connecting users isn't a billing event on Fabriq, and making calls isn't one on Nango's free tier. Onboard forty design partners who each connect one tool and Nango's free plan runs out while Fabriq's doesn't. Run a batch job that hits one connected account a hundred thousand times and the reverse is true.


## Whose OAuth App You Register


This is the biggest single difference in time to first tool call, and it rarely makes it into a comparison table.


We had this section wrong, and the correction is worth more than the original claim. Nango's auth guide does open with "OAuth APIs require an OAuth developer app registered with the provider" — but the very next sentence is "If the API has a Nango-managed OAuth app, you can use it and skip the rest of this step," and its managed-app section now states flatly: "Nango-managed OAuth apps can be used in production." When we first published this page on 2026-10-12 we quoted a line recommending you register your own app before going live. That line is not on the page we read on 2026-10-29. So Nango is *not* asking you for a Cloud project before your first call, and we should not have implied it was.


What Nango does instead is publish the honest tradeoff list for a shared app, which is better practice than a recommendation anyway. Register your own, it says, if any of these matter: "Whitelabel auth — with a Nango-managed app, the consent screen shows Nango, not your product"; fixed scopes, where "Your own app can request any scope the provider offers"; a custom callback URL on your domain; provider marketplace listings; and first-party-only API features.


Two more are worth quoting in full. "Revocation risk — most providers don't allow shared credentials. If a provider revokes a Nango-managed app, every connection using it stops working." And portability: "only with your own app can you export access and refresh tokens and move off Nango without users re-authorizing." Nango also notes these "apply to shared OAuth apps from any auth platform, not just Nango", which includes ours. Every item on that list is true of our shared apps too.


For production Nango also recommends an endpoint on your own domain that 308-redirects to` https://api.nango.dev/oauth/callback` , so the callback domain your users see belongs to you, and it warns that retrofitting that later can break authorization flows.


Fabriq's catalogue lists three connection methods per provider: Agentic Fabriq's OAuth app, your own OAuth app, and a credential your user supplies. Ours comes with a plan boundary rather than a recommendation. On the Free plan you bring your own OAuth app. On Launch or Growth our shared apps cover non-restricted scopes after a one-time attestation, which includes Calendar, Sheets, Docs, Slack and Notion. Gmail and full Google Drive are restricted scopes under Google's policy and go through your own Google app on every plan — so if Gmail is your integration, you are in Google's verification queue on either platform, and the honest version of this section is that neither of us can make that go away.


Where Nango is better here, plainly: portability. With your own client on Nango you can export access and refresh tokens and leave without making your users reconnect. Our external-user flow has no raw-token export path at all, which is a security property on purpose and a lock-in cost in practice.


**Figure 1 — Neither path requires provider paperwork to start: Nango ships managed OAuth apps usable in production, and ours cover non-restricted scopes on a paid plan. The paperwork comes back for a restricted scope, for whitelabel consent, or for token portability.**


On the Fabriq side the code is short enough to quote. You install` agentic-fabriq-sdk` for Python or` @agenticfabriq/sdk` for TypeScript, put` AF_APP_ID` and` AF_APP_SECRET` in the environment, and call two methods:


python


```text
from     af_sdk     import     AgenticFabriq


af   =   AgenticFabriq  ()                       # reads AF_APP_ID / AF_APP_SECRET


url   =   await     af  .  initiate_connection  (  request  ,   provider  =  "gmail"  )     # send the user here


async     with     await     af  .  for_user  (  request  )   as     session  :
tools   =   await     session  .  get_tools  ()      # only what this user granted
result   =   await     session  .  call_tool  (  "google_gmail_list_messages"  , {  "max_results"  :   5  })
```


Note what isn't in that snippet: a user id. Both calls take your framework's request object and read identity from the session your own auth already established, because a user id as a parameter is a value your code, or a model inside it, can get wrong or invent. The escape hatch for background jobs is spelled` dangerously_use_raw_user_id` , which is hard to type by accident and easy to grep for.


Nango's equivalent is a connect session created from your backend, returning a` connect_link` valid for 30 minutes, then an agent session whose tenant you express with connection tag selectors. Those have to resolve to exactly one connection per integration or creation fails with` ambiguous_connections` . Good design, and one more concept to learn on a Friday.


## Catalogue Size, Stated Plainly


Both vendors publish a headline number, and both numbers mean less than they look like.


Nango's repository and docs say 1,000+ APIs, with new ones "added on demand within days, by request or self-contributed". Its pricing page on 2026-10-29 advertises "Auth for 1,000+ APIs" and "10,000+ tools, one server" — up from the "7k pre-built tools, triggers & syncs" we read on 2026-10-12. The contribution path is real and is part of why that number keeps moving.


Fabriq's catalogue currently holds 511 providers and 62,678 catalogued actions. Of those, 125 have a live OAuth sign-in, 12 have OAuth in progress, and 374 have no OAuth flow at all and connect by credential instead; 87 can run on our own provider app and 116 accept an OAuth app you register. Those are counts out of the generated catalogue file in our own codebase, not marketing, and we'd rather you read them here than discover them halfway through an integration.


There's a tighter number that matters more here. The end-user *OAuth* flow, the one where your customer clicks a link and signs in at the provider, drives thirteen providers end to end today: Gmail, Google Drive, Docs, Sheets, Slides, Calendar, Meet, Forms, Contacts and Chat, plus Slack, GitHub and Notion. Anything else returns a 400 from the initiate endpoint.


Everything else goes through a credentials page we host, and we had this wrong too. An earlier version of this page said that page supported Notion only and that every other key-based connector was connected by you in a console. Our developer documentation now says the opposite and says it emphatically: there is no admin-entered credential path for external users, and 448 of the 511 providers reach that hosted page — 444 where your user supplies a credential, 4 (WhatsApp, Instagram, LinkedIn, Telegram) where they complete the provider's own sign-in instead. The ticket lives in the URL fragment, is single-use, expires in five minutes, allows three attempts, and the credential is probed against the provider before it is stored.


**If your product needs your users to self-connect a long tail of niche SaaS tools through a provider sign-in this quarter, Fabriq Developer is the wrong tool and Nango is the right one.** Thirteen OAuth providers is thirteen, however large the catalogue and the credentials page behind them.


## Self-Hosting, With the Asterisk


Nango being open source is the reason a lot of developers shortlist it, so it's worth being precise about what that gets you in October 2026.


The repository's LICENSE file is the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI open source. Its central limitation reads: "You may not provide the software to third parties as a hosted or managed service, where the service provides users with access to any substantial set of the features or functionality of the software." For almost every product team that's irrelevant, since you're embedding integrations in your own app rather than reselling Nango. Anyone planning to offer an integration layer to their own customers as a service should read it twice.


The self-hosting docs list three paths: BYOC, where "Nango deploys and operates your instance inside your own AWS account, GCP project or Azure subscription"; Self-Managed, where "you deploy and operate Nango yourself, on your own infrastructure, using our Helm chart"; and Free Self-Hosted, "a limited free self-hosting option is available for hobby projects". Read the feature table before you plan around it. Free Self-Hosted covers API Auth, the Proxy, and observability limited to "Auth + proxy only". Syncs, tool calls, webhooks, triggers, the MCP server, RBAC, MFA, SAML SSO and the audit trail all need Enterprise self-hosting or Nango Cloud.


Read that against what you probably wanted it for. If you came to Nango because you want an agent tool layer running inside your own VPC for free, the free build has no MCP server and no tool calls. That's in the docs rather than hidden in a changelog, but it isn't what "open source and self-hostable" suggests to a developer skimming a README.


Fabriq's position here is worse on paper and we'll say it flatly. There is no public source to read and no free self-host. Installing into your own Kubernetes cluster on AWS or GCP via our Helm chart is available on a custom plan, which means talking to us. If self-hosting is a hard requirement at seed stage, Nango wins this section outright.


## The Shape of a Tool


Here the two architectures stop resembling each other, and it's where we'd spend the most evaluation time.


In Nango, a tool is an action function. The docs are unambiguous: "Only action functions can be tools." You enable a template function on an integration or write and deploy your own, and it runs provider-specific code with the connected account's credentials. Agent sessions expose a chosen subset of those functions over an MCP server at a per-session` mcp_url` , authenticated with a` session_token` . Sessions are immutable, can't be extended, default to 15 days, and die on a` DELETE` , after which that MCP server answers 401.


The context handling there is genuinely good. By default nothing in the toolset is listed;` tools/list` returns Nango's meta tools plus whatever you explicitly pinned, paginated 50 at a time, and the agent finds the rest with a` nango_tool_search` meta tool. That keeps a large toolset out of a context window it would otherwise fill with definitions the model never calls. One documented sharp edge: Nango warns that with the` nango_proxy` meta tool enabled, "the agent can call any endpoint of a connected integration in the toolset, including ones your deny list was meant to keep out." Leave it off unless you need it.


The trade is that the tool surface is code you own, so it's also code you maintain. Nango gives you real tooling for that: dry runs, mocks, snapshot tests, a CI/CD path, plus syncs with a records cache, checkpoints and deletion detection if what you need is replicated provider data rather than live calls. Fabriq has nothing comparable to syncs. If your roadmap says "RAG over the customer's Drive, refreshed hourly", that's a Nango job.


Fabriq's tool surface is served from the gateway instead. One schema per tool, one MCP endpoint, and the effective tool list for a call is the intersection of what the user granted and what the agent is scoped to. The agent holds a short-lived session token, 900 seconds by default with a one-hour ceiling, re-minted 60 seconds before expiry, so calling` for_user` per request is the intended pattern rather than waste. The TypeScript SDK stops short of wrapping an MCP client: it hands you` token` and` mcpUrl` and expects you to bring your own. Some will read that as unfinished. We think it's right for a layer that shouldn't own your agent loop, and it's still one fewer convenience than Nango's Node SDK.


## Who Holds the Token


Credential model is one of the nine dimensions in the[agent access control taxonomy](https://agenticfabriq.github.io/agent-access-control-taxonomy/) , and it's where these two products' defaults point in opposite directions.


Nango encrypts credentials with AES-256-GCM under an envelope scheme whose data key is wrapped by AWS KMS, which is a solid build, and it's SOC 2 Type II certified with a HIPAA BAA on an add-on. It also hands them back. The auth guide's second code sample is` nango.getConnection(integrationId, connectionId)` , described as how you "fetch credentials whenever you need them". Functions and the proxy let you avoid that, and agent sessions state plainly that "the agent never sees raw credentials, and cannot change the scope of its own session". But pulling the live access token into your own backend is a first-class documented path, which puts your logs, your error reporting and your incident response in scope for it.


Fabriq's default runs the other way. In proxy mode the credential stays in the vault and is attached server-side at the moment of the call, so the agent gets a session and never the secret. Every token also records an` auth_level` for how the user was proven:` app_asserted` means we took your app's word for it,` app_signed` means your backend signed a 60-second single-use assertion with a private key we never hold, and` user_present` exists only for a moment after a human finished a connection and can't be renewed. You can require signed assertions and refuse unsigned token requests outright. One thing we don't do: disconnecting clears the grant held in our own vault and nothing more. If you need Google to forget, ask Google.


**Figure 2 — Both platforms can do both shapes. The difference is which one the documentation puts first, and defaults decide what most teams ship.**


Neither default is wrong. If you're writing integration code yourself you need the token, and Nango handing it over is the feature. With an LLM in the loop we'd keep the secret out of any process the model can influence, which is why proxy mode is our default rather than our option.

## Which to Choose


No single winner here.


**Choose Fabriq Developer when** your free-tier ceiling should be calls rather than connected users — forty design partners on one tool each is the case that breaks Nango's free plan and not ours; when identity should come from the session your own auth established rather than a tenant selector your code resolves; when you want the credential to stay out of the agent's process by default rather than by discipline, with no retrieval API to misuse; when the providers you need sit in the Calendar, Sheets, Docs, Slack, Notion or GitHub cluster; or when you want per-call audit records on a free plan rather than on an Enterprise one.[Fabriq Developer](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/developers) and the[Developer Quickstart](https://www.agenticfabriq.com/docs/dev-quickstart) are the two pages to read next, in that order.


**Consider Nango when** self-hosting is a hard requirement — this is its clearest advantage and we have no answer to it below a custom plan. Also when you want integration code you own and can read; when you need provider data replicated into your own store with change detection, which we have no equivalent for at all; when token portability matters, because only Nango lets you export access and refresh tokens and leave without making users reconnect; when your provider list runs into the long tail of B2B SaaS where a provider sign-in matters; or when your users must see your brand on the consent screen and a custom callback URL on your own domain.


**Pick both** is not a cop-out: Nango for syncs and owned integration code, Fabriq for the agent-facing tool surface. They don't fight. Think hard before running two credential stores, though. That's two breach surfaces.


## Frequently Asked Questions


**Is Nango open source?** The repository is public and its LICENSE file is the Elastic License 2.0, which is source-available rather than OSI open source. You can read, modify and run it, but not offer it to third parties as a hosted service providing "any substantial set of the features or functionality of the software".


**Can I self-host Nango for free?** Yes, with a limited feature set. The docs describe the free option as being "for hobby projects", covering API Auth and the Proxy. Syncs, tool calls, webhooks, triggers and the MCP server require Enterprise self-hosting or Nango Cloud.


**Can I self-host Agentic Fabriq?** Only on a custom plan, via a Helm chart into your own Kubernetes cluster on AWS or GCP. No free self-hosted build, no public source. Nango is ahead here.


**Do I have to register my own OAuth app?** On neither platform, to start. Nango's auth guide says "Nango-managed OAuth apps can be used in production" and publishes the tradeoffs of a shared app rather than a recommendation against it. On Fabriq, our shared provider apps cover non-restricted scopes on a paid plan after a one-time attestation; on the Free plan you bring your own; and Gmail and full Google Drive use your own Google app on every plan because Google treats those scopes as restricted. (An earlier version of this answer said Nango recommends registering your own app before going live. That line is no longer on its auth guide, and the correction is in Nango's favour.)


**How many integrations does each have?** Nango advertises "Auth for 1,000+ APIs" and "10,000+ tools, one server". Fabriq's catalogue holds 511 providers and 62,678 catalogued actions: 125 with a live OAuth sign-in, 374 that connect by credential. The end-user OAuth flow drives thirteen of them end to end, and 448 providers reach the hosted credentials page your user fills in.


**Which free tier goes further?** It depends on the axis. Nango gives you 10 connections, 10 compute hours and 10GB a month, and its managed OAuth apps are usable in production. Fabriq gives you 20,000 calls a month and unlimited agents with no per-user charge, but no access to our shared provider apps until a paid plan. Forty design partners fit on one and not the other; a whitelabel-free launch with no OAuth registration fits on the other and not the one.


**Does either stop an agent calling a tool it shouldn't?** Both narrow the surface. Nango's sessions take an allow and deny toolset and the agent can't change its own scope. Fabriq's effective tool list is the intersection of the user's scopes and the agent's, computed when the list is built and again at call time. Neither replaces not granting write access you don't need.


## Conclusion


These two look similar in a feature grid and feel nothing alike in practice, because they sit on opposite sides of one decision. Nango hands you the materials: your OAuth app, your function code, your records cache, optionally your own infrastructure. Fabriq hands you an endpoint and keeps the materials.


At pre-seed the cost of the first option is almost never the subscription. It's the afternoon learning a function runtime and the decision about whose OAuth app to register, both spent before you know whether anyone wants the feature. The second option bills you later, as a ceiling you hit when the provider you need isn't in the thirteen, when you want our shared apps on a free plan, or when a customer asks to see their own name on the consent screen.


**Our advice, and we're not neutral:** start with whichever one gets a real tool call returning real data today, then write down the one fact that would force you to switch. "We need our own consent screen." "We need Xero." "We need this in our VPC." A named trigger beats a six-month architecture argument.
